terminal_objective: Given any legal board position, correctly identify all legal moves available to a specified pawn.
performance_context: During a game, a player must decide whether a pawn can advance, capture, or is blocked before committing to a move.

learning_objectives.statement: State the conditions under which a pawn may move one or two squares forward.
Distinguish between a pawn's movement direction and its capture direction.
Given a board position, determine whether a pawn is blocked, free to advance, or able to capture.

concepts.name: Forward movement
concepts.definition: A pawn moves one square forward toward the opponent's side of the board. It cannot move sideways or backward.
concepts.elaboration: White pawns move from lower rank numbers to higher (e.g. rank 2 toward rank 8). Black pawns move in the opposite direction. A pawn cannot move forward if any piece — regardless of colour — occupies the square directly in front of it.

misconceptions.misconception: A pawn can move backward to return to safety.
misconceptions.correction: Pawns never move backward under any circumstances. Once advanced, they cannot retreat.

misconceptions.misconception: A pawn can jump over a piece blocking its path.
misconceptions.correction: Pawns cannot jump. If the square directly ahead is occupied, the pawn is completely blocked and has no forward move.

concepts.name: Initial two-square advance
concepts.definition: A pawn that has not yet moved may advance two squares forward in a single move, provided both the square it crosses and the destination square are unoccupied.
concepts.elaboration: This option is only available once per pawn, from its starting rank (rank 2 for White, rank 7 for Black). If either intervening square is occupied, the two-square advance is not legal, even if only the middle square is blocked.

misconceptions.misconception: A pawn can move two squares forward from any position.
misconceptions.correction: The two-square advance is only available from the pawn's starting rank. Once it has moved at all, it may only advance one square at a time.

misconceptions.misconception: A pawn can leap over a piece on the first square to land on the second.
misconceptions.correction: Both squares must be empty. If the first square is occupied, the pawn cannot advance at all — it cannot jump to the second square.

concepts.name: Diagonal capture
concepts.definition: A pawn captures by moving one square diagonally forward. It can only capture in this way — it cannot capture a piece directly in front of it.
concepts.elaboration: A pawn captures to either of the two squares diagonally ahead of it. An opponent's piece on one of those squares may be captured. A pawn cannot capture a piece that is directly in front of it — that piece simply blocks the pawn's advance.

misconceptions.misconception: A pawn can capture the piece directly in front of it.
misconceptions.correction: This is the most common pawn misconception. A pawn cannot capture forward. The piece in front blocks the pawn's advance; it does not become a capture target.

misconceptions.misconception: A pawn must capture if a diagonal capture is available.
misconceptions.correction: Captures are never forced in chess unless the alternative leaves the king in check. A player may choose not to capture with a pawn.

cases.title: The blocked pawn
cases.setup: White has a pawn on e4. Black has a pawn on e5. Both pawns face each other on the same file.
cases.decision_point: Can the White pawn on e4 advance or capture?
cases.correct_action: The White pawn cannot move. The square directly in front of it (e5) is occupied by a Black pawn, which blocks forward movement. There are no Black pieces on d5 or f5 to capture.

incorrect_actions.action: Advance to e5, capturing the Black pawn.
incorrect_actions.why_wrong: Pawns cannot capture forward. The piece directly ahead blocks movement; it is not a capture target.

incorrect_actions.action: Advance to e5 as a normal move, pushing the Black pawn back.
incorrect_actions.why_wrong: Pieces in chess do not push each other. An occupied square cannot be entered except by a legal capture, and pawns do not capture forward.

cases.title: The starting pawn's choice
cases.setup: White has a pawn on d2 (its starting square). The squares d3 and d4 are both unoccupied. A Black knight sits on e3.
cases.decision_point: What moves are available to the White pawn on d2?
cases.correct_action: The pawn may advance one square to d3, or two squares to d4. The Black knight on e3 is one rank ahead and one file to the right — a valid diagonal capture square — so the pawn may also capture by moving to e3.

incorrect_actions.action: Advance to d4 only, assuming the two-square advance skips d3.
incorrect_actions.why_wrong: The two-square advance does not skip the middle square. Both d3 and d4 must be empty — if d3 were occupied, d4 would also be unavailable.

cases.title: The available capture
cases.setup: White has a pawn on c4. Black has a bishop on d5. The square c5 is empty.
cases.decision_point: Can the White pawn capture the Black bishop?
cases.correct_action: Yes. The Black bishop on d5 is one square diagonally forward of the White pawn on c4. The pawn may move to d5, capturing the bishop.

incorrect_actions.action: Decline to capture because the pawn can only move straight ahead.
incorrect_actions.why_wrong: Pawns capture diagonally forward — this is their only means of taking an opponent's piece. A pawn on c4 with an opponent's piece on d5 is a legal capture opportunity.

assessment_items.stem: White has a pawn on e4. Black has a rook on e5. There are no other pieces adjacent to the White pawn. What can the White pawn do?

options.text: Capture the Black rook by moving to e5.
options.feedback: Pawns cannot capture forward. The Black rook on e5 is directly in front of the pawn, which means it blocks the pawn's advance — it does not become a capture target.
options.misconception_targeted: A pawn can capture the piece directly in front of it.

options.text: The pawn is blocked and has no legal move.
options.feedback: Correct. A pawn cannot move forward into an occupied square, and it cannot capture forward. With no opponent pieces on d5 or f5, the pawn has no legal move from e4.

options.text: Advance to e6, jumping over the Black rook.
options.feedback: Pawns cannot jump over other pieces. Unlike the knight, a pawn's path must be clear. If e5 is occupied, the pawn cannot advance to e6 or any square beyond.
options.misconception_targeted: A pawn can jump over a piece blocking its path.

options.text: Retreat to e3 to avoid being captured.
options.feedback: Pawns never move backward. Once advanced, a pawn cannot retreat regardless of the threat it faces.
options.misconception_targeted: A pawn can move backward to return to safety.

assessment_items.stem: White has a pawn on g2. The square g3 is occupied by a White knight. The square h3 is empty. Which of the following correctly describes all legal moves for the White pawn?

options.text: The pawn can advance to g3 or g4.
options.feedback: The White knight on g3 blocks the pawn completely. Since g3 is occupied, the pawn cannot advance to g3, and because the two-square advance requires both g3 and g4 to be empty, it cannot reach g4 either.
options.misconception_targeted: A pawn can leap over a piece on the first square to land on the second.

options.text: The pawn can advance to g4 by jumping over the White knight on g3.
options.feedback: Pawns cannot jump. The White knight on g3 blocks the pawn's path entirely — the pawn cannot skip g3 to reach g4.
options.misconception_targeted: A pawn can jump over a piece blocking its path.

options.text: The pawn has no legal forward moves and no captures available.
options.feedback: Correct. The White knight on g3 blocks the pawn's forward advance entirely, including the two-square option. The pawn could only capture by moving diagonally to f3 or h3 if an opponent's piece occupied one of those squares — but both are empty, so no capture is available.

options.text: The pawn can capture the White knight on g3 to clear its path.
options.feedback: A pawn cannot capture its own pieces — only opponent's pieces can be captured. Additionally, the pawn cannot capture forward in any case; captures are always diagonal.
options.misconception_targeted: A pawn can capture the piece directly in front of it.
